lesson.title: Electroconvulsive Therapy: Modern Practice Behind an Old Reputation
lesson.summary: Electroconvulsive therapy uses brief, controlled electrical stimulation of the brain under general anesthesia to treat severe depression that has not responded to other treatments, and modern ECT bears little resemblance to the frightening, inaccurate depictions many people picture.
lesson.body:
Electroconvulsive therapy, or ECT, is a medical procedure in which a carefully controlled electrical current is used to briefly stimulate the brain and induce a short seizure. It is performed under general anesthesia with a muscle relaxant, so the patient is unconscious and their body does not visibly convulse during the procedure. ECT is most often considered for severe major depressive disorder that has not adequately responded to other treatments, such as the psychotropic medications discussed earlier in this unit and psychotherapy, and it is sometimes used in other situations where a more rapid response is medically necessary.

Much of the public's image of this treatment comes from outdated portrayals dating back decades, before modern anesthesia and safety practices were standard, showing it as frightening, painful, or used without a patient's informed consent. These depictions do not reflect how ECT is practiced today. Modern ECT is administered by a trained medical team, with the patient unconscious throughout the brief procedure and vital signs closely monitored, and treatment is typically given as a series of sessions spread over several weeks, not as a single dramatic event.

Research has generally found ECT to be among the more effective available treatments for severe depression that has not responded to other approaches. As with the other treatments described in this unit, it is not effective for every person, and it is generally reserved for more severe or treatment-resistant cases rather than used as a first option.

Possible side effects can include short-term confusion and some memory disruption around the time of treatment. The extent and duration of these effects vary from person to person, and researchers continue to study ways to minimize them. Deciding whether ECT is appropriate for a given person is a careful medical decision made between a patient, or their decision-makers, and their treatment team, and this chapter is meant to explain how the treatment generally works, not to advise on that decision.

Like several other treatments described in this unit, ECT shows how a legitimate, carefully studied medical treatment can still carry an outdated reputation shaped by history rather than current practice. Understanding how it actually works today is part of engaging with mental health treatment accurately rather than through myth.
